slots.text: Most founders think user interviews are about validating their idea. They're actually about invalidating your assumptions. Big difference.

Three things that kill idea validation:

1. Asking leading questions
2. Talking to friends who lie to be nice
3. Confusing polite interest with buying intent
The hardest part of building with AI isn't the tech. It's figuring out which manual processes are actually worth automating. Most workflows exist for good reasons you don't see until you remove them.
Every founder says they want to remove friction. But when you watch users actually struggle with your product, you realize friction often exists because clarity doesn't.
User feedback falls into two buckets: what they say they want, and what they actually pay for. The second bucket is smaller and more expensive to fill.

Signs you're talking to the wrong users:

1. They love everything about your idea
2. They have unlimited time to chat
3. They've never paid for a solution
4. They want features, not outcomes
Most founders think validation means asking 'would you use this?' The real question is 'what's broken about how you do this today?' If they can't articulate the pain, your solution doesn't matter.

User interviews that actually work:
1. Ask about their current process, not your idea
2. Listen for workarounds they've built
3. Find the thing they complain about to coworkers
4. Ask what they tried before that didn't work

The hardest part about building with AI isn't the tech stack. It's that users expect magic but need predictability. They want it to read their mind but also want to know exactly what it's going to do. Threading that needle is brutal.
Founders who remove one manual step from their own workflow this week will learn more about product-market fit than founders who survey 100 strangers about their hypothetical idea.
Every workflow has that one stupid step everyone just accepts. Find it, fix it, charge for it. Half of successful startups are just someone who refused to accept 'that's how we've always done it.'

Signs your idea validation is actually working:
1. People interrupt you to tell you their problems
2. They ask when they can start using it
3. They volunteer to help you test it
4. They send you screenshots of their current broken process
Most founders skip validation because they're afraid of hearing 'no.' But getting a clear 'no' is infinitely more valuable than a polite 'maybe' that wastes six months.

Three questions that actually matter in user interviews:

1. What's the last time this problem cost you money?
2. What workarounds are you using right now?
3. Who else deals with this at your company?

Everything else is noise.
The AI tools paradox: everyone wants to 'build with AI' but most founders haven't identified which parts of their workflow actually need automating. We're solving for technology instead of problems.
Founders who talk to 5 users get confident. Founders who talk to 50 users get paranoid. The paranoid ones build better products.
Friction isn't always bad. Sometimes it's the only thing preventing your users from making expensive mistakes. Remove the right friction, keep the guardrails.

Signs you're validating wrong:

1. You're asking hypothetical questions
2. You're talking more than listening
3. You're interviewing your friends
4. You haven't changed your idea yet

At least one of these is you.
Most founders skip validation because they think users will lie to them. They will. But the lies tell you more about what they actually want than any direct answer.

3 signs your AI feature is solving the wrong problem:
1. Users ask how to turn it off
2. Support tickets increase after launch
3. Everyone says it's 'cool' but usage drops after day 2

Every workflow tool promises to remove friction but most just move it around. You're not eliminating steps, you're hiding them behind setup wizards and configuration screens. The friction is still there, just wearing a different hat.
Users who immediately ask about pricing are usually tire kickers. Users who ask about implementation timelines are usually buyers.
The best user interviews happen when you forget you're doing a user interview. Stop reading from your script and start being curious about their actual day.

4 ways to validate an idea without building anything:
1. Sell it before you build it
2. Manual service first, automate later
3. Fake the AI with humans behind the scenes
4. Use existing tools to mimic your solution
Most founders skip validation because they're afraid their idea isn't special enough to survive contact with reality. But ideas that can't survive user feedback weren't worth building anyway.

Three ways to know you're talking to the wrong users:

1. They love everything you show them
2. They ask when it'll be free
3. They suggest features for completely different problems

Pain recognition beats politeness every time.

AI tools keep promising to eliminate manual work, but they're creating new categories of manual work instead. Now we're manually prompting, manually reviewing outputs, manually connecting systems that used to just work.
Founders who've been through YC have a specific way of describing problems: they lead with the user, not the solution. Everyone else starts with 'So we built this thing that...'
Removing friction sounds good until you realize some friction is intentional. The three-click purchase flow isn't broken design—it's preventing buyer's remorse and chargebacks.

Workflow automation red flags:

1. Takes longer to set up than doing it manually for 6 months
2. Breaks every time someone updates a field name
3. Requires a dedicated person to maintain it
4. Creates more notifications than it eliminates
Most founders skip validation because they think talking to 10 users takes forever. It takes 3 hours. Building the wrong thing for 6 months takes forever.

Red flags when validating ideas:
1. Everyone says it's a "great idea" but won't commit to using it
2. Users describe the problem but can't tell you their current workaround
3. The pain point only exists during your interview
4. They ask about pricing before features
The hardest part of user interviews isn't getting people to talk. It's shutting up long enough to hear what they're actually saying instead of what confirms your assumptions.
Founders who build with AI first usually create solutions looking for problems. Founders who validate problems first use AI to solve them faster.
Removing friction isn't about fewer clicks. It's about fewer decisions. Every choice you force users to make is a place they can quit.

Questions that actually matter in user interviews:
1. Show me how you handle this now
2. What's the worst part about your current process
3. How much time/money does this problem cost you
4. What would have to be true for you to switch
Most founders skip validation because they think their idea is obviously good. The obvious ones usually aren't.

Three things that kill user interviews:

1. Leading questions that confirm what you want to hear
2. Asking about hypothetical future behavior
3. Talking more than listening

Shut up and let them tell you their problems.

Building with AI feels like having a really smart intern who occasionally hallucinates. You can move fast but you're constantly babysitting the output. Not sure if this gets better or if we just get better at working around it.
Founders who talk about 'removing friction' usually add three new steps while fixing one old problem. The workflow gets smoother in theory, messier in practice.
User feedback is not a democracy. Five people saying they want a feature doesn't mean you should build it. Listen for the problem, not the solution.

Signs your validation is actually just confirmation bias:

1. You only talk to people who already like your idea
2. You explain the problem before asking if they have it
3. You count 'that sounds cool' as validation
4. You ignore everyone who says no
